content: 1. Countries should systematically collect standardized data on sentinel events and indicators, ensuring at least the inclusion of six key cascade events as outlined in the guidelines. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides specific guidance on key indicators for paper-based monitoring systems and additional indicators for electronic systems or periodic reviews, particularly for patient monitoring tools. 2. HIV case surveillance must ensure de-duplication of records to provide accurate counts of diagnosed individuals and those receiving treatment. This data should be shared with healthcare facilities to enhance reporting accuracy and support facility operations. WHO offers guidance on implementing these de-duplication approaches. 3. Improvements in HIV surveillance, patient monitoring, and the use of unique identifiers should be guided by a country-specific situation analysis. This analysis should identify and estimate the costs of incremental improvements. WHO provides tools to assist countries in conducting such analyses. 4. HIV case surveillance should begin with the diagnosis of HIV and build upon existing patient monitoring systems. WHO provides detailed guidance on HIV case definitions to support this process. 5. Data routinely collected can be utilized to assess access to services by key populations. However, confidentiality and security are critical when collecting data related to key populations, whether through patient monitoring or HIV case surveillance systems. In most settings, patient monitoring records should not include key population categories, and any collected information should primarily support patient management and referrals to care. 6. Unique identifiers should be promoted and used in HIV patient records and data shared within national HIV programs. These anonymous codes should be securely linked to individual health records. WHO provides definitions and examples of unique identifiers to guide implementation. 7. Countries should progressively transition from paper-based to electronic patient information systems, particularly in facilities managing more than 2,000 patients. WHO offers a tiered approach as an example for this transition. 8. Different levels of data security should be assessed and established for various data elements. Investments should be made in robust databases and policies to ensure data security and confidentiality, tailored to the risks and benefits in specific settings. WHO provides major headings and references for additional specialized guidance. 9. Countries should invest in secure and interoperable data systems. Strengthening the interoperability of electronic databases and adopting open-source standards for data systems is essential. WHO recommends allocating 5–10% of the program budget to enhance monitoring and evaluation systems. 10. Individual-level data should be used to improve programs and long-term chronic healthcare. WHO emphasizes linking data to program improvements and collecting evidence of these improvements. This includes strengthening retention and transfer of care by routinely sharing information between clinics, ensuring linkage between testing, treatment, laboratory, pharmacy, and other health services, and integrating HIV services with broader chronic healthcare using unique identifiers. 11. Investments should be made in data analyst capacity, including central and district-level analysts, and in routine dashboards to provide real-time feedback for program improvement. 12. Feedback from consultations with countries during the development of these guidelines highlighted the importance of strengthening existing data systems and utilizing the data they collect. Improvements should not be introduced as separate monitoring or surveillance systems but should aim to progressively strengthen and integrate patient monitoring, case surveillance, and the use of unique identifiers to link data within HIV programs and health systems. 13. People-centered monitoring should prioritize patient benefits, and patients should be consulted during its development. The guidelines should ideally align with the timing of reviews of monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems in countries, based on a country situation analysis that reviews current systems, identifies incremental improvements and costs, and assesses data security, confidentiality, and potential patient and program benefits. 14. The first investments should focus on strengthening and securing information systems and using the data to demonstrate program benefits. This stage should enhance data security and usage, provide real-time feedback to decision-making at all levels, and document benefits. 15. The sustainability of the system and its links to health and national data systems should be planned for the short, medium, and long term, based on a review of benefits and costs. This maturation pathway should address the sustainability of human resources, financing, policies, interoperability, open access, and the integration of HIV services with the broader health system. Evidence of program benefits, risks, and a maturation plan for investments should be developed in consultation with key stakeholders.
